metadata.title: Reverse De La Riva Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Reverse De La Riva Guard Bottom in BJJ. Complete guide covering sweeps, back takes, and transitions. Success rates: Beginner 45%, Intermediate 60%, Advanced 75%.

overview:
Reverse De La Riva Guard Bottom is an advanced open guard position where the bottom player inverts their De La Riva hook, threading their near leg through the opponent's far leg from behind while maintaining control of the opponent's opposite leg. This creates a powerful off-balancing system that specializes in back takes, waiter sweeps, and kiss of the dragon entries. Unlike traditional De La Riva, which focuses on leg entanglements and direct sweeps, Reverse De La Riva excels at creating angles that expose the opponent's back.

The position requires strong hip mobility and core strength to maintain the inverted hook structure. It's particularly effective against standing opponents or those attempting to pass around the hooking side. The guard has become increasingly popular in modern competition due to its effectiveness at creating immediate back-taking opportunities, which are highly valued in both gi and no-gi grappling. The position serves as a critical bridge between traditional open guards and modern leg entanglement systems, offering practitioners multiple pathways to dominant positions.

Strategically, Reverse De La Riva operates on the principle of creating rotational off-balancing that forces opponents to make defensive choices, each of which opens different offensive opportunities. The inverted hook structure naturally pulls the opponent's base in a circular pattern, making it difficult for them to establish stable posture or initiate effective passing sequences. This makes it particularly effective in gi grappling where pant and ankle grips can enhance the control, though the core mechanics translate effectively to no-gi when proper hand positioning replaces fabric grips.

Hips elevated off the mat with active core engagement, creating dynamic mobility rather than static positioning on the shoulders or lower back
Far leg controlling opponent's opposite side through hooking behind knee or gripping ankle, preventing them from stepping away or establishing stable base
Active hook pressure maintained through both legs with constant push-pull tension that keeps opponent off-balance and unable to settle into defensive posture
Shoulders turned toward opponent with upper body positioning that prevents back exposure while maintaining visual contact and grip control
Near-side hand controlling opponent's far ankle or pant leg while far-side hand frames against near leg or hip to maintain distance management
prerequisites: Strong hip mobility for maintaining inverted hook position with sustained elevation
Understanding of basic De La Riva guard mechanics and off-balancing principles
Core strength for sustained hip elevation and dynamic movement
Familiarity with back-taking sequences and crab ride mechanics
Ability to transition fluidly between open guard variations
Grip fighting proficiency for establishing and maintaining ankle and pant controls
key_principles: Hip Elevation: Keep hips off the mat to maintain mobility and pressure, using core engagement to create dynamic rather than static positioning
Inverted Hook Control: The reversed De La Riva hook creates unique rotational off-balancing angles that expose the opponent's back
Far Leg Management: Controlling opponent's far leg prevents escape and creates sweep opportunities while maintaining the guard structure
Shoulder Positioning: Keep shoulders turned toward opponent to prevent back exposure while maintaining offensive options
Dynamic Tension: Maintain active push-pull pressure with both legs to keep opponent constantly reacting and off-balance
Angle Creation: Use hip movement to create angles for back attacks, particularly through rotation under the opponent
Grip Fighting: Strategic grips on ankles and pants enhance control and create pathways to sweeps and back takes

common_errors.error: Keeping hips flat on the mat without active elevation
common_errors.consequence: Reduces mobility and eliminates the off-balancing pressure that makes the position effective, allowing opponent to easily control distance and initiate passes. Static hip positioning also makes it impossible to generate the rotational movement needed for back takes.
common_errors.correction: Actively elevate your hips off the mat by engaging your core and maintaining tension in your hook structure, creating dynamic pressure that keeps opponent off-balance. Think of your hips as the steering wheel that controls the direction of the sweep or back take. Recognition: If you feel static or unable to generate movement, your hips are likely too flat.

common_errors.error: Losing far leg control during transitions
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to step away with their far leg, establishing distance and stable base from which they can initiate passing sequences or completely disengage from the guard. Without far leg control, the inverted hook loses its off-balancing power.
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant awareness of far leg control through hooks or grips, adjusting between ankle control and knee control based on opponent's position. If you lose the hook, immediately transition to a grip or re-establish control before attempting offensive techniques. The far leg control is what prevents opponent escape and creates the leverage for sweeps.

common_errors.error: Allowing shoulders to turn away from opponent
common_errors.consequence: Exposes your back and eliminates offensive options, transforming you into a defensive position where opponent can attack your turtle or establish top control. Turning away also breaks the visual connection needed to read opponent's reactions and time your attacks.
common_errors.correction: Keep shoulders square to opponent with chest facing toward them, maintaining visual contact and hand positioning that controls distance. Your upper body should always be engaged with opponent through grips and frames, never turning to expose your back unless executing a deliberate inversion technique.

common_errors.error: Static hook positioning without dynamic adjustment
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to adapt to your pressure and establish counter-pressure, neutralizing the off-balancing effect of the inverted hook. Static hooks are easy to defend and don't create the dilemmas that force opponent into vulnerable positions.
common_errors.correction: Constantly adjust hook depth and angle based on opponent's weight distribution, using push-pull motion to keep them reacting. The inverted hook should feel like a constant wave of pressure rather than a fixed anchor point. Vary between deep hooks around the thigh and shallow hooks on the calf based on what creates the most off-balancing effect.

common_errors.error: Gripping opponent's far ankle without controlling their near leg
common_errors.consequence: Creates an imbalanced control system where opponent can easily drive their near knee forward to smash pass or establish headquarters position. The far ankle grip alone is insufficient to prevent skilled passers from working around the inverted hook.
common_errors.correction: Use your far leg to control opponent's near leg (either hooking behind their knee or establishing a frame on their hip) while your hand grips their far ankle. This creates a diagonal control system that prevents them from driving forward or stepping away. Both sides of the control structure must work together to create effective off-balancing.

common_errors.error: Attempting sweeps or back takes without establishing proper grips first
common_errors.consequence: Results in failed techniques where you lose guard position without gaining sweep or back control, often ending in opponent achieving the pass. Premature attacks without grip control leave you vulnerable to counter-passing sequences.
common_errors.correction: Always establish your grip control system (typically far ankle and near leg control) before initiating dynamic movements. The grips should feel secure and connected before you commit your hips to a sweep or inversion. If opponent is actively fighting your grips, focus on grip fighting first before attempting offensive techniques.

training_drills.name: Hook Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to extract their leg from your inverted hook while you maintain the structure with progressive resistance (25%, 50%, 75%), focusing on hip mobility and hook pressure. Partner varies their escape attempts between backstepping, forward pressure, and lateral movement. Emphasize keeping hips elevated and maintaining constant tension in the hook throughout all their defensive movements.
training_drills.duration: 5 minutes per round, 3 rounds alternating roles

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Drilling
training_drills.description: Flow between waiter sweep, kiss of the dragon, and crab ride entries based on partner's weight distribution, developing recognition of which technique to apply in each situation. Partner provides realistic resistance and weight shifts to simulate competition scenarios. Focus on reading their weight distribution and immediately selecting the highest percentage technique without hesitation.
training_drills.duration: 10 minutes continuous flow, rotating partners every 2 minutes

training_drills.name: Far Leg Control Practice
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to step away with their far leg while you maintain control using hooks and grips, alternating between ankle control and knee control to understand both options. Partner progressively increases their escape attempts from 50% to 100% intensity. Develop the sensitivity to feel when to transition between different control methods based on their movement patterns.
training_drills.duration: 3 minutes per control type, 2 rounds each

training_drills.name: Dynamic Hip Movement Drill
training_drills.description: From established Reverse De La Riva position, practice elevating and rotating hips in circular patterns while maintaining hook structure. Partner remains passive initially, then gradually adds resistance. Focus on generating momentum through hip movement that creates off-balancing angles without losing the fundamental guard structure.
training_drills.duration: 5 minutes per round, building from 0% to 75% resistance

expert_insights.danaher: The Reverse De La Riva guard represents a sophisticated evolution in open guard theory, utilizing inverted hook mechanics to create rotational off-balancing that is biomechanically difficult to counter. The fundamental principle operates on the concept that by threading your leg through the opponent's stance from behind, you create a leverage system where their natural defensive responses actually increase the effectiveness of your attacks. When they drive forward to pressure your guard, they feed directly into the waiter sweep. When they attempt to disengage by standing or backstepping, they expose their back to kiss of the dragon entries. The position creates what I call a 'rotational dilemma' where every defensive choice leads to a specific offensive opportunity. The key technical element is maintaining hip elevation, which transforms the position from a static guard into a dynamic launching platform for attacks. Your hips must remain elevated and mobile, never settling flat to the mat, as this elevation is what generates the momentum for inversions and back takes. The inverted hook itself should be understood as a steering mechanism that controls the opponent's center of gravity in a circular pattern, making it nearly impossible for them to establish the linear base needed for effective passing.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I use Reverse De La Riva as a primary back-taking entry in competition, particularly against opponents who are proficient at defending traditional De La Riva. The waiter sweep is my highest percentage technique from here, as it forces the opponent into a compromised position whether they defend by staying heavy or by trying to backstep. The key is maintaining constant tension in the hook system and never allowing your hips to flatten out. In no-gi, the position works even better because opponents can't use pants grips to stabilize, making the off-balancing extremely effective. My approach is to establish the inverted hook immediately when opponent stands in my De La Riva, then quickly assess their weight distribution to determine whether I'm going for the sweep or transitioning to kiss of the dragon. Against high-level opponents, I often use the position as a transitional state rather than holding it for extended periods - the goal is to create immediate off-balancing that leads to back exposure within 2-3 seconds of establishing the hook. The far leg control is absolutely critical; if you lose that control even momentarily, skilled passers will immediately capitalize by stepping away and establishing distance. I drill the transition between RDLR and Single Leg X constantly because opponents will often backstep to defend the waiter sweep, and that backstep motion feeds perfectly into Single Leg X entries where you can continue attacking with sweeps or leg locks.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Reverse De La Riva fits perfectly into the 10th Planet system's emphasis on back attacks and unconventional entries. We connect it directly to the crab ride and truck positions, creating a seamless chain from guard to back control. The inverted hook creates confusion for opponents who are drilling traditional passing sequences, and the hip mobility required develops naturally when you're also training rubber guard and lockdown variations. I teach students to view this as a transitional position rather than a static guard, always looking to roll under for the back or sweep to top position within a few seconds of establishing the hook. The beauty of RDLR in our system is how it complements the lockdown game - if you're comfortable inverting and using unconventional hip positions in lockdown, the mechanics of RDLR feel natural. We also combine it with our electric chair setups, where the inverted hook can be used to off-balance opponent before transitioning to deep half or lockdown positions. The key innovation in our approach is using the RDLR not just for sweeps and back takes, but as an entry point into leg lock positions and truck mechanics. When opponent defends the traditional RDLR attacks, we have drill sequences that transition to saddle entries or outside ashi positions, creating a multi-layered offensive system where they can't focus on defending just one attack type. The position embodies the 10th Planet philosophy of constant movement and unconventional angles that keep opponents guessing.

overview: Reverse De La Riva Guard (RDLR) is a modern guard variation that emerged as a counter to specific passing strategies, particularly the knee cut and leg drag passes. The position is characterized by the bottom player hooking the opponent's non-passing leg with their outside leg, while the inside leg creates a frame across the opponent's hip or thigh. RDLR serves as both a defensive position to prevent passes and an offensive launching pad for sweeps, back takes, and transitions to other guards, making it a crucial component of the modern guard system. The position gained prominence in the early 2000s as competitors developed sophisticated counter-passing systems, with practitioners like Cobrinha, Miyao brothers, and other berimbolo specialists demonstrating its offensive potential for creating back exposure opportunities.
state_invariants: Outside leg (far leg) hooking deeply behind opponent's far knee, with foot positioned near opponent's inner thigh or hip, creating strong rotational control and preventing forward pressure
Inside leg (near leg) establishing active frame against opponent's near hip or thigh, with knee shield or butterfly hook positioning to manage distance and prevent chest-to-chest pressure

Upper body angled approximately 45 degrees relative to opponent, with shoulders off the mat and spine curved to maintain mobility and prevent flattening, creating dynamic positioning rather than static defense
Grip control established on opponent's far sleeve/wrist or far collar, coordinating with the outside leg hook to create rotational control and off-balancing opportunities
Near-side hand controlling opponent's belt, hip, or pants at the knee to manage distance and facilitate transitions to offensive sequences

Familiarity with inversion mechanics and back exposure techniques

key_principles: Hook opponent's non-passing leg deeply with outside leg, maintaining tension and rotational control
Frame actively against opponent's passing hip with inside leg to manage distance and prevent consolidation
Control opponent's far sleeve/wrist or collar with far-side arm to disrupt posture and create off-balancing
Establish belt/hip grip with near-side arm to manage distance and facilitate sweeps or inversions
Maintain angled spine positioning (approximately 45 degrees) to prevent flattening and preserve mobility
Create and exploit leverage through coordinated hook tension and frame pressure

common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily clears hook with hand or hip pressure, consolidating passing position and eliminating guard retention options

common_errors.consequence: Loss of distance management and guard retention as opponent establishes heavy chest pressure, flattening defender and preventing hip mobility necessary for sweeps or inversions

common_errors.error: Focusing solely on defensive hook maintenance without developing offensive sequences

common_errors.correction: Constantly threaten offensive transitions (berimbolo, sweeps, X-Guard entries) to force opponent into defensive reactions that create openings for guard retention and advancement

common_errors.error: Poor grip management with loose or disconnected upper body controls
common_errors.consequence: Loss of posture disruption and rotational control, allowing opponent to establish strong base and execute passes without dealing with off-balancing threats

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish crossface or underhook without immediate counter-response

common_errors.correction: Immediately address crossface attempts with frame creation and underhook battles with whizzer or re-guard movements, preventing opponent from establishing passing grips

expert_insights.danaher: The Reverse De La Riva Guard represents the evolution of guard systems from purely defensive structures to integrated offensive platforms. The position's true value lies not in static maintenance but in its capacity to create systematic pathways to superior positions, particularly back control through berimbolo mechanics. The key technical principle involves understanding that RDLR functions as a transitional hub rather than a destination - the outside leg hook creates rotational control that disrupts opponent's passing base while the inside frame manages distance to prevent consolidation. When these two control points work in coordination with proper grip fighting on the upper body, you create a three-dimensional control system that simultaneously defends passes while threatening back exposure. The biomechanical advantage emerges from the fact that your outside hook attacks opponent's furthest leg, creating maximum leverage for off-balancing, while your inside frame addresses their nearest point of pressure. This creates a dilemma where opponent must simultaneously defend rotational attacks and forward pressure management. Advanced practitioners recognize that RDLR serves as the gateway to the entire modern guard ecosystem - X-Guard, Single Leg X, and various inversion-based back takes all flow naturally from properly established RDLR position. The systematic approach involves first mastering retention mechanics under pressure, then progressively adding offensive sequences as technical proficiency develops.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In modern competition, RDLR has become one of the most essential guard positions because it directly addresses the two most common passing approaches - knee cut and leg drag - while simultaneously creating immediate back attack opportunities. From a practical standpoint, I use RDLR primarily as an offensive launching pad rather than a defensive holding position. The moment I establish the RDLR hook and inside frame, I'm already thinking about berimbolo entries, kiss of the dragon inversions, or X-Guard sweeps depending on how my opponent reacts. The competition reality is that static RDLR maintenance against elite passers is extremely difficult, but dynamic RDLR with constant offensive threats forces opponents into reactive rather than proactive passing, which fundamentally changes the engagement. My approach emphasizes grip fighting intensity - I want far sleeve control and belt/hip control established before I commit to RDLR positioning, because without these grips the position becomes purely defensive. The highest percentage path from RDLR in competition involves berimbolo variations to back control, which is why you see elite competitors like the Miyao brothers and Cobrinha building entire game plans around this sequence. The key detail most practitioners miss is that RDLR requires constant hip movement and angle adjustment - you cannot remain static and expect the position to work against high-level opposition. Every passing attempt should be met with immediate counter-movement toward offensive sequences, creating a dynamic exchange where you're always threatening progression even while defending.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: RDLR fits perfectly into the 10th Planet philosophy of creating positions that work equally well in gi and no-gi contexts, though the grip variations obviously change significantly. In no-gi, we focus heavily on underhook and overhook controls combined with the RDLR hook structure, creating what I call 'mission control variations' that blend RDLR mechanics with rubber guard concepts. The beauty of RDLR in the 10th Planet system is how it connects to our calf slicer entries, truck position pathways, and electric chair setups from the inversion sequences. Where traditional gi-based RDLR emphasizes berimbolo to back control, we've developed parallel pathways that lead to leg entanglements and calf compression attacks that work better in submission-only formats. The critical innovation we've added involves using RDLR as a recovery position from failed lockdown attempts or as a transition hub when opponents defend our standard half guard attacks. The no-gi grip fighting becomes about wrist control, overhook battles, and strategic use of the whizzer to prevent opponent from establishing crossface or underhook positions that bypass RDLR structure. I teach students to view RDLR as part of a continuous guard flow rather than isolated position - you might hit RDLR momentarily during transitions between butterfly, X-Guard, and deep half, using it as a control point to redirect opponent's passing momentum into submission or back attack opportunities. The submission-only competition format has proven that RDLR works exceptionally well for creating leg lock entries, particularly when opponents stand to pass and expose their legs to outside ashi garami transitions from the same hook position that creates RDLR structure.

overview:
Reverse De La Riva Guard Top represents the passing perspective against one of modern BJJ's most dynamic and versatile guard systems. The top player faces a bottom opponent who has established a reverse De La Riva hook (instep of one foot behind the knee while the same-side hand controls the ankle), creating a complex entanglement that can lead to sweeps, back takes, or leg attacks. The primary objective from top is to systematically dismantle the guard structure through proper base, pressure distribution, and strategic movement while avoiding common traps like the kiss of the dragon sweep or berimbolo entries.

This position requires sophisticated understanding of weight distribution, as the bottom player's reverse De La Riva hook creates a lever system designed to off-balance and invert the top player. Success from top position depends on maintaining connection to the mat through strategic posting, preventing the bottom player from getting underneath your center of gravity, and systematically removing the guard's structural components in the correct order. The modern meta-game heavily emphasizes headquarters positioning, where the top player creates a mobile base that can pressure while remaining prepared to address dynamic guard retention attempts.

The top player must navigate multiple decision points: whether to engage in smash passing protocols, float passing methodologies, or leg drag systems. Each pathway requires different pressure patterns and grip configurations. Understanding the relationship between the reverse De La Riva hook's mechanical advantage and your own base positioning is crucial, as improper weight distribution leads directly to sweeps or scrambles. The position serves as a critical junction in modern guard passing sequences, particularly in no-gi competition where reverse De La Riva has become a foundational guard retention tool.
state_invariants: Top player maintains standing or combat base position with at least one foot posted on the mat for structural stability, preventing bottom player from elevating hips above top player's center of gravity

Bottom player has established reverse De La Riva hook with instep of one foot positioned behind top player's near-side knee, creating a lever system that connects through the ankle grip on the same side

Top player's weight distribution must account for the reverse De La Riva hook's pulling vector, requiring strategic posting and pressure angles to maintain balance and prevent inversion or kiss of the dragon entries
Bottom player's far leg (non-hooking leg) typically posts on top player's hip, bicep, or remains in space as a framing tool, creating distance management and preventing immediate smash passing
Top player's grips focus on controlling bottom player's pants at the knees or ankles, or establishing collar/cross-face controls to limit bottom player's upper body mobility and inversion capacity
prerequisites: Bottom player has successfully established reverse De La Riva hook structure with proper ankle control
Top player is in standing, combat base, or headquarters position with ability to maintain balance against the hook's leverage
Sufficient space exists between players to allow the reverse De La Riva hook mechanics to function
Top player has not yet passed the guard or established dominant pressure positions like leg drag or knee slice
Bottom player maintains active guard retention with far leg and upper body positioning to prevent immediate passing
key_principles: Maintain strategic base positioning with weight distributed to counter the reverse De La Riva hook's sweeping vector, typically requiring posting on the hooking-side leg while keeping hips back
Control the distance between your hips and bottom player's hips to prevent them from getting underneath your center of gravity, which enables kiss of the dragon and berimbolo entries
Strip the reverse De La Riva hook methodically by attacking the ankle grip first, then addressing the hook itself through backstep, leg drag, or smash passing protocols
Establish headquarters position or similar mobile base that allows pressure application while maintaining readiness to address dynamic guard retention movements
Use collar ties, cross-faces, or pants grips to limit bottom player's ability to invert and access back exposure or leg entanglement transitions
Progress through passing stages systematically: neutralize the hook, establish control position (headquarters/leg drag), then complete the pass to side control or mount
Recognize and defend common sweeps (kiss of the dragon, technical standup sweep, berimbolo) by maintaining proper posture and weight distribution throughout the passing sequence

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to drift too far forward over bottom player's center of gravity
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can easily execute kiss of the dragon sweep or berimbolo entry by getting underneath your base
common_errors.correction: Keep hips back with active posting on the hooking-side leg, maintaining distance between your center of gravity and bottom player's hips

common_errors.error: Pulling up on bottom player's reverse De La Riva hook to remove it
common_errors.consequence: Creates elevation that assists bottom player's sweeping mechanics and can lead to technical standup sweeps or inversion entries
common_errors.correction: Address the ankle grip first through wrist control or grip breaks, then use backstep or lateral movement to neutralize the hook

common_errors.error: Standing too upright with poor base width
common_errors.consequence: Provides unstable platform that bottom player can easily off-balance through reverse De La Riva hook leverage
common_errors.correction: Maintain wide base with strategic posting, keeping weight distributed to counter the hook's sweeping vector

common_errors.error: Ignoring bottom player's far leg (non-hooking leg) positioning
common_errors.consequence: Allows bottom player to maintain distance and create effective frames that prevent passing pressure
common_errors.correction: Control the far leg through knee grips, push it across to create passing lanes, or pin it to prevent effective framing

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass directly into the reverse De La Riva hook without neutralizing it
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains guard structure and can transition to other guards or sweep attempts
common_errors.correction: Use systematic hook removal through backstep, leg drag, or smash passing protocols before attempting final passing sequences

common_errors.error: Over-committing to one passing direction without reading bottom player's adjustments
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can anticipate and counter your passing attempts through guard retention or transition to other guards
common_errors.correction: Maintain mobile headquarters position with ability to switch passing directions based on bottom player's reactions

common_errors.error: Neglecting upper body control (collar ties, cross-face) while focusing only on leg positioning
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can freely invert, access back exposure, or create scramble situations
common_errors.correction: Establish upper body controls early to limit bottom player's inversion capacity while addressing lower body entanglements

training_drills.name: Reverse De La Riva Hook Removal Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player establishes reverse De La Riva guard. Top player practices systematic hook removal through backstep, grip breaking, and lateral movement without allowing bottom player to sweep or invert. Progress through 5 repetitions each side, focusing on maintaining balance and proper base throughout the sequence. Bottom player provides 50% resistance initially, increasing to 75% as top player develops timing.

training_drills.name: Headquarters to Pass Progression
training_drills.description: Start from reverse De La Riva guard top position. Top player must achieve headquarters position first, then choose one of three passing pathways: leg drag, knee slice, or smash pass. Bottom player actively attempts guard retention using reverse De La Riva hook, far leg frames, and inversion attempts. Reset when pass is completed or bottom player successfully sweeps. Perform 10 total repetitions alternating between passing options.

training_drills.name: Inversion Defense Positioning Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player establishes reverse De La Riva guard and actively attempts berimbolo or kiss of the dragon entries. Top player focuses solely on maintaining proper base positioning, hip distance, and backstep timing to prevent successful inversion. No passing attempts—drill emphasizes defensive positioning only. Perform 3-minute rounds with active bottom player, resetting to reverse De La Riva after each successful defense.

training_drills.name: Grip Fighting and Ankle Control Drill
training_drills.description: Isolated drill focusing on the battle for ankle control in reverse De La Riva guard. Bottom player attempts to maintain ankle grip while top player uses wrist control, grip breaks, and hand fighting to remove it. Once ankle grip is broken, reset to reverse De La Riva with grip established. Perform 2-minute rounds focusing on hand speed, grip strength, and strategic grip placement.

training_drills.name: Dynamic Passing Against Multiple Guard Transitions
training_drills.description: Bottom player can transition freely between reverse De La Riva, X-Guard, Single Leg X, and De La Riva variations. Top player must recognize each guard, apply appropriate passing pressure, and complete passes despite guard transitions. This drill develops pattern recognition and adaptive passing strategies. Perform 5-minute rounds with goal of completing 3-5 passes per round.

expert_insights.danaher: The reverse De La Riva guard from the top perspective represents a fascinating study in leverage mechanics and base geometry. The fundamental problem you face is that the bottom player has created a lever system through their reverse De La Riva hook that mechanically advantages them in the sweeping exchange. Your hook-side leg becomes the fulcrum point, and their hook creates a pulling vector designed to rotate you around that fulcrum. The solution lies not in fighting the lever directly, but in removing its mechanical advantage through systematic deconstruction. First, address the ankle grip—this is the bottom player's steering mechanism for the hook. Without ankle control, the hook loses much of its directional capability. Second, create distance between your hips and their hips. The closer your center of gravity drifts to being directly above theirs, the easier their sweeping mechanics become. Maintain this distance through strategic posting on your hooking-side leg while keeping your hips back. Third, use the backstep as your primary defensive framework against inversion attempts. When the bottom player begins to invert for berimbolo or kiss of the dragon entries, the backstep removes you from the danger zone while simultaneously positioning you in headquarters, a superior passing platform. The entire sequence should be understood as a systematic removal of structural components: grip, then hook, then completion of pass. Each stage requires specific technical protocols, and attempting to skip stages leads directly to sweeps or scrambles.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: From a competition standpoint, reverse De La Riva top is all about controlling the pace and not giving them the reactions they want. Most reverse De La Riva players are hunting for you to commit your weight forward or try to pull up on their hook—both reactions lead directly to their offense. Instead, I focus on maintaining a mobile headquarters position where I can pressure their guard structure without giving them the balance disruptions they need. My primary goal is to strip the ankle grip early, usually through wrist control or by pinning their gripping hand to their own body. Once that grip is gone, the hook becomes much less dangerous and I can start working my passing sequences. I heavily favor the leg drag from here because it addresses both the hook and creates passing lanes simultaneously. The key is staying patient and not forcing passes before I've properly neutralized their guard structure. Against high-level reverse De La Riva players, I'm also constantly aware of the berimbolo threat. The moment I feel them starting to invert or get their shoulders to the mat, I'm stepping back to headquarters and resetting. You can't let them get underneath you. In terms of actual passing completion, I find that combinations work best—threaten the leg drag, when they defend, switch to knee slice or smash pass. The reverse De La Riva player's defensive reactions to one passing attempt often create openings for different passes. Competition data shows that successful passing from reverse De La Riva top correlates strongly with grip fighting success and maintaining proper hip distance throughout the sequence.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Reverse De La Riva top is where you see the evolution of the guard passing game in real time, especially in no-gi where this guard has become absolutely fundamental. From the 10th Planet perspective, we approach this position with an understanding that the bottom player is trying to create chaos—they want you off-balance, they want scrambles, they want to access your back. Our counter-strategy focuses on staying in our base and using what we call 'headquarters lockdown mode' where we're pressuring but ready to bail at any second. The reverse De La Riva hook is basically a trap waiting for you to make the wrong movement, so we drill extensively on recognizing the sweep setups before they happen. One thing that's often overlooked is the importance of the far leg (the leg that's not hooked)—controlling that leg or at least being aware of how they're using it for frames and distance management is critical. We also emphasize the backstep as a defensive art form. When they start inverting for the berimbolo or kiss of the dragon, that backstep needs to be automatic and smooth, not panicked. The innovation in passing reverse De La Riva lately has been in the combination game—you can't just commit to one passing direction anymore against good players. You need to be able to flow between leg drag, knee slice, and smash passing based on their defensive adjustments. We drill this as a decision tree where each defensive reaction they make opens up a specific passing lane. The position really rewards creativity and pattern recognition over pure strength or pressure.
